content: The provision of non-clinical services should be carried out promptly to minimize the morbidity and mortality associated with HIV infection. This approach aims to enhance overall health outcomes and improve the quality of life for individuals. Additionally, it is essential to promote the efficient and effective use of available resources. The consolidated guidelines on the use of antiretroviral drugs for treating and preventing HIV infection emphasize several key considerations for integrating quality improvement (QI) into national HIV care policies, programs, and strategic plans. These include: 1. Stakeholder Involvement: Engage stakeholders, including networks of people living with HIV, communities, and healthcare workers, to build a shared understanding of strengthening the quality of HIV care services and optimizing resource use. 2. Policy and Strategy Elements: Identify components of national policies and strategies that address the quality of HIV care services, as well as HIV-related stigma and its impact on access to care. 3. Prioritization of Quality Assurance (QA) and QI: Develop and implement strategies for QA and QI in HIV care. 4. Monitoring Indicators: Establish nationally harmonized key indicators and reporting requirements to monitor the quality of HIV care services. 5. Defined Roles and Responsibilities: Clearly define the roles and responsibilities of stakeholders at various levels of the healthcare delivery system to strengthen the quality of HIV care services. 6. Resource Allocation: Allocate resources to develop mechanisms that support QI, including management and information systems for reporting, monitoring, and improving the quality of HIV care services. Align performance with evidence-based best practices. 7. People-Centered Care: Incorporate high-quality, people-centered HIV care delivery into the principles, values, and strategies of national policies and HIV strategic plans. 8. National Standards: Set evidence-based standards for HIV care through national guidelines, defining the package of services to be offered, the level of the healthcare delivery system, and the target population or geographic location. The guidelines also provide operational guidance on procurement and supply management (PSM) systems, focusing on how these systems can adapt to new recommendations. This must be achieved in the right quantities, at the lowest possible cost, and in a timely manner. The recommendation to initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART) for all people living with HIV, regardless of CD4 cell count, necessitates an integrated national strategic response. This response should consider available resources and strengthen PSM systems at all levels of the health system. The scaling up of ART programs will require collaboration between procurement managers and ART program managers to forecast, procure, and distribute the necessary quantities of ARV drugs and other health commodities to meet increasing national demand and achieve the 90–90–90 targets. Key steps in building a strategy for continuous quality improvement include: Assessment and Evaluation: Involve stakeholders, conduct a situation analysis to identify gaps, and confirm set goals. Strategies: Define goals for quality improvement and select appropriate interventions. Implementation: Execute the implementation process and monitor progress. While there are no major changes in the recommended ART regimens, new drugs are suggested as components of alternative regimen choices, which may have implications for PSM. Unplanned adoption of these recommendations could lead to stock-outs and imbalances in drug and diagnostic supplies. Challenges and opportunities in implementing new WHO recommendations include product selection, demand forecasting, procurement planning, global supply capacity, storage and distribution logistics, monitoring consumption, and managing costs. National HIV programs should establish stakeholder working groups to address these issues, involving policymakers, implementers, PSM specialists, and representatives from central medical stores and finance ministries. Medicines should be selected based on national ART guidelines and program needs, minimizing the number of ARV drug regimens to optimize treatment and sourcing. Drugs no longer recommended by WHO should be removed from national guidelines, and patients should transition to more effective regimens. National procurement programs should consolidate PSM systems, consider pooled procurement mechanisms, and establish long-term framework contracts to reduce transaction costs and improve delivery schedules. Storage and distribution plans should include quality assurance of products upon receipt, secure storage facilities, cold storage for temperature-sensitive products, inventory control systems, and regular distribution patterns. Monitoring systems should capture accurate consumption data to prevent stock-outs and overstocking, ensuring program flexibility and avoiding expired health products. To avoid stock-outs, close coordination with HIV program managers and policymakers is essential to align the pace of ART scale-up with the availability of required commodities. Quantification and ordering should include a rotating safety buffer to compensate for forecasting errors and delivery delays. Orders should be placed well in advance, with a recommended lead time of at least six months to allow for production and cost-effective shipping. National HIV programs should also consider supply chain adaptations to support new service delivery models, such as less frequent ARV drug refills, community ART delivery, and lay providers distributing ARV drugs. A phased approach should account for additional ARV drug needs, storage capacity, reporting requirements, and shelf-life constraints.
